transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-08-04 16:30 UTC
Duration: 46 minutes (approx)
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Marco Alvarez (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Lara Chen (Redwood SE), Tom Whitaker (CTO - Catalyst), Jamal Ortiz (Head of MLOps - Catalyst), Aisha Khan (PM), Maya Singh (Security)
Recording URL: https://redwood.zoom/rec/ff-20260804-ctc-3917 (note: link mocked)

Auto-summary: Medium-quality transcript. Focus: cost/unit economics, deployment options, security constraints.

[00:00] Marco (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining — Marco from Redwood here, with Priya and Lara on the call. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Tom (Catalyst): Good, thanks. Quick note, we've got about 45 minutes, tight schedule.
[00:12] Marco: Perfect — objective for today is to understand your budget constraints and workloads so we can map hosted vs dedicated vs private options.
[00:20] Jamal: Yeah, high level: we're running a mix of chat assistants and embedding search. For chat, 80% small prompts ~75 tokens, 20% long context ~1.2k tokens. Embeddings are batches of 10–50 texts. Monthly budget target is effectively capped — we can't exceed $20k/mo for inference initially.
[00:40] Priya (Redwood): Got it. Are you tracking token volumes today or is this a rough estimate?
[00:45] Jamal: Rough estimate. We have logs but they need cleaning. Expect peak concurrency around 400 qps for short prompts during trading hours; average is probably 120 qps.
[01:00] Lara (Redwood): Ok, good detail. Two levers that usually move the needle are batching for embeddings and prefix/KV caching for chat. Even simple prefix caching can save 30–50% on repeated system prompts.
[01:18] Aisha (Catalyst): Quick clarification: when you say caching, do you mean Redwood handles the KV cache server-side or that we need to implement application-side caching?
[01:26] Priya: Redwood offers automatic KV/prefix caching in the runtime as an optional feature for hosted and dedicated; for private, you can choose to run it locally or let Redwood's control plane manage the cache metadata. The wording sometimes gets fuzzy — apologies if past notes said 'K-V cache' or 'KV store' differently.
[01:43] Tom: Important point — we cannot have any PII leaving our VPC for the pilot. So private deployment or VPC-hosted control plane are must-discuss.
[01:52] Maya (Catalyst): Also SOC 2 and detailed audit logs are required for our vendor review.
[01:58] Marco: Understood. We support SOC 2, SSO/SAML, and we can integrate with your KMS (HSM options as well). We'll share the SOC2 report and VPC checklist after the call.
[02:10] Jamal: Great. Back to costs — how should we think about per-token pricing vs per-instance reserved costs? For our kind of workload, is dedicated clearly cheaper?
[02:22] Priya: Short answer: it depends on utilization profile. If you can sustain consistent GPU utilization — e.g., high percentage of reserved minutes — dedicated reserve tends to lower per-token cost because the amortized infra cost drops. But if your workload is spiky or uncertain, hosted with auto-burst can be more predictable and avoids long-term commit.
[02:41] Marco: Also, we provide suggested batching configs and quantization profiles per model. For embeddings, batching 32–64 can give large per-call savings. For chat, dynamic batching and KV cache usually matter more.
[02:56] Tom: Any ballpark numbers for comparison? Even roughs help us present to finance.
[03:02] Priya: For example, for a Llama-ish 13B class model: hosted single-token price might land at N cents/token (we should send the exact table), while dedicated amortized could be 30–60% cheaper at steady state depending on GPU type and utilization. Important caveat: those numbers change with sequence length distribution and whether you use int8 or int4 quantization.
[03:25] Jamal: Int4 sounds interesting but we worry about quality regressions.
[03:29] Lara: We include recommended eval prompts and expected delta metrics when suggesting quantization; typically for retrieval-augmented chat, int8 is safe, int4 needs validation. We'll share a report.
[03:44] Aisha: If we go dedicated, what's the minimum commitment? Procurement wants to know contract lengths and exit clauses.
[03:50] Marco: Standard dedicated contracts are monthly with annual discounts for 12-month commits. We can structure a pilot-friendly agreement — short initial commit with rights to scale up or down with notice. We'll coordinate legal.
[04:02] Tom: Another question — network egress costs and cross-zone latency. We have multiple regions and need <150ms p95 for chat in EU and US. Can Redwood guarantee that?
[04:12] Priya: We operate regional endpoints and can route by policy. For p95 under 150ms, we typically recommend dedicated in-region pools, and prefix caching reduces token compute time — but tail latency also depends on queuing and batch sizes. For strict SLAs we have Dedicated with SLA options.
[04:29] Jamal: Do you have examples of customers who moved from hosted to dedicated and the economics?
[04:33] Marco: Yes — we'll anonymize a couple of case studies: one fintech that reduced per-token unit cost by ~40% after committing to dedicated and using a combination of batching and KV caching. We'll add that to the follow-up package.
[04:47] Tom: Procurement will ask about security — do you support customer-managed keys and full audit trails?
[04:53] Lara: Yes, KMS integrations for private and dedicated; hosted can also support customer-managed keys via BYOK. Audit logs and per-token tracing are available in the console with configurable retention.
[05:05] Aisha: What's the typical turnaround to stand up a private deployment in our environment (vpc + peering)? Three to six weeks?
[05:12] Priya: For VPC-hosted private deployments, typical timeline is 2–4 weeks for a basic pilot if networking is straightforward; on-prem/air-gapped can be longer due to hardware procurement. We'll include a checklist to accelerate networking approvals.
[05:25] Jamal: On the topic of batch sizing — for embeddings, if we batch 64, what happens to latency?
[05:30] Priya: There's a tradeoff: batching increases throughput and reduces cost per embedding, but wall-clock latency per request can increase due to batching waits. For offline embedding jobs it's a no-brainer, for real-time embedding APIs we suggest adaptive batching with a small time window to cap latency.
[05:45] Marco: Also worth noting: caching repeated queries mostly affects chat where system messages and few staples repeat; embedding caching is less common unless exact text repeats.
[05:55] Tom: Financially, if we hit the $20k/mo cap, what are options — throttling, graceful degradation?
[06:01] Marco: We have quota enforcement and routing policies. You can set budget-based routing: route to cheaper quantized variants or to smaller models when budget threshold hits, or enable automatic fallbacks to cached responses. Those policies can be configured per route.
[06:18] Maya: For compliance, any data resident restrictions? We need logs stored in EU for EU customers.
[06:24] Lara: Yes, we can configure region-specific storage and log retention. For private deployments you control storage entirely.
[06:34] Jamal: Let's sketch a sample unit-econ calculation live — say 2M short-chat tokens/day and 0.5M long-chat tokens/day, embeddings 200k per month.
[06:42] Priya: Ok quick calc: short-chat average 75 tokens * 2M = 150M tokens; long-chat 1200*0.5M = 600M tokens. Total 750M tokens/month for chat. Embeddings are charged separately often per-embedding unit — 200k embedding calls, assume batch sizes average 25 -> 8k BPU (batch processing units) — rough. If hosted per-token price is X, multiply out; if dedicated, amortize GPU cost over total tokens, add storage and networking. We'll send a modeled spreadsheet.
[07:18] Tom: Sounds good — please include tail-latency assumptions.
[07:22] Marco: Will do.
[07:24] Aisha: Any red flags you see with our profile?
[07:27] Priya: Two things: 1) if your peak concurrency is very spiky (400 qps peaks) you might waste reserved capacity unless you use burst pools; 2) embedding pipelines should be batched aggressively to meet budget. Otherwise, sounds feasible within $20k with some combination of dedicated baseline and hosted burst.
[07:47] Jamal: What's the effort to integrate single-sign on and RBAC?
[07:51] Lara: We support SAML/SSO and OIDC; RBAC is configurable per team in the console. For private installs we can mirror your identity provider.
[07:59] Tom: Procurement timeline — likely to sign pilot doc in 2–3 weeks if we like the numbers. Security review might take longer.
[08:06] Marco: Great. Recap: we'll send cost modeling, SOC2 + VPC checklist, bench plan, and case studies. Any other items?
[08:14] Maya: Please include a note on BYOK and HSM options.
[08:18] Marco: Noted.
[08:20] Priya: We'll propose a bench run where we run your sample traffic against a candidate model for up to 4 hours to capture p95/p99 and real cost. That gives you actual numbers.
[08:31] Tom: That would be helpful.
[08:33] Marco: Ok, let's set a tentative bench slot next Tuesday; we'll confirm by email.
[08:38] Jamal: One more quick tech Q: do you support model pinning and automatic fallback to a smaller variant on overload?
[08:44] Lara: Yes, model pinning and policy-based fallback are first-class — can fallback to quantized or smaller family automatically.
[08:50] Aisha: Good.
[08:53] Marco: Anything else from anyone?
[08:55] Tom: No, thanks — good call.
[08:58] Marco: Thanks all. We'll follow up with the packet and calendar invite for bench test.
